stem: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with oral discomfort and a persistent white coating in his mouth for the past 1 week. He reports recent use of broad-spectrum antibiotics. On examination, there are multiple white plaques on the oral mucosa that can be gently scraped off, revealing an erythematous underlying surface. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
keywords: “Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus” → strong risk factor for opportunistic fungal infection (immunocompromised state).
“Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics” → disrupt normal oral flora → overgrowth of Candida species.
“White plaques that are easily scraped off leaving erythematous base” → classic diagnostic feature of pseudomembranous oral candidiasis.

A.title: Oral candidiasis
A.body:
White plaques in the oral cavity that are creamy, curd-like, and easily removable with scraping strongly suggest fungal overgrowth. The underlying mucosa appears erythematous due to inflammation.
Common in immunocompromised patients like diabetics and after antibiotic use.
Caused by Candida albicans proliferation due to disrupted normal flora.
This is the classic “thrush” presentation and the most likely diagnosis in this case.
A.clinicalReasoning: The combination of immunosuppression (diabetes), antibiotic use, and scrapable white plaques makes this a textbook presentation of pseudomembranous candidiasis. The lesion’s reversibility with scraping is the most distinguishing feature.

B.title: Oral leukoplakia
B.body: This is a premalignant condition characterized by a persistent white patch that cannot be scraped off. It is strongly associated with smoking and chronic irritation. Unlike candidiasis, it does not show an erythematous base after removal because it is firmly adherent epithelial dysplasia. It carries malignant transformation risk.
B.clinicalReasoning: The key differentiating point is non-scrapability. Since the lesion in this case is removable, leukoplakia is excluded.

C.title: Oral lichen planus
C.body: A chronic inflammatory mucocutaneous disorder presenting with bilateral white lacy reticular patterns (Wickham striae). It is immune-mediated and often associated with burning sensation rather than removable plaques. Lesions are typically persistent and not scrapable.
C.clinicalReasoning: Absence of reticular “lace-like” pattern and presence of scrapable plaques makes this unlikely.

D.title: Oral hairy leukoplakia
D.body: This condition is associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection, commonly seen in HIV patients. It presents as corrugated, non-scrapable white plaques on the lateral tongue. It is not associated with diabetes or antibiotic use.
D.clinicalReasoning: Location (lateral tongue), EBV association, and non-scrapability distinguish it from candidiasis.

E.title: Oral squamous cell carcinoma
E.body: A malignant lesion often presenting as a non-healing ulcer, indurated mass, or mixed red-white lesion. It is usually non-scrapable and progressive, often linked with tobacco and alcohol use.
E.clinicalReasoning: Acute onset, scrapable nature, and infection-related risk factors make carcinoma unlikely in this case.

keyConcept: Oral candidiasis is an opportunistic fungal infection seen in immunocompromised states such as diabetes mellitus and after antibiotic use. Its hallmark feature is scrapable white curd-like plaques with an erythematous base, which differentiates it from leukoplakia and other non-scrapable oral white lesions.

diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the clinical recognition, pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of oral candidiasis (oral thrush), a common opportunistic fungal infection caused by Candida albicans. It highlights major risk factors such as diabetes mellitus, recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use, immunosuppression, and poor oral hygiene. The hallmark feature demonstrated is the presence of white curd-like oral plaques that can be scraped off to reveal an erythematous base. The infographic also summarizes diagnostic confirmation with KOH mount showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae, along with antifungal treatment approaches including topical and systemic therapy.
